threats.description: An attacker impersonates a trusted entity (ECU, user, or backend service) to gain unauthorized privileges or inject false data. This is the abstract base class for all spoofing threats.

threats.name: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attack
threats.description: An attacker intercepts and alters communications between two entities without their knowledge, breaking secure channels.

elapsedTime.rationale: Establishing an on-path position and forcing or exploiting a channel-security weakness (rogue AP, ARP spoofing, or CA misuse) is achievable within days to weeks of reconnaissance.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Defeating TLS/PKI validation or performing a live protocol downgrade requires genuine applied-cryptography and network-protocol expertise, though not multiple combined disciplines.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: TLS/DTLS and PKI are public standards; only the target's specific certificate-pinning or trust-chain configuration is non-public.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A rogue Wi-Fi AP or ARP-spoofed local segment gives an easily obtainable interception window; no rare timing condition is required.

equipment.rationale: Commodity MITM proxy tooling (mitmproxy, rogue AP hardware) is sufficient; no bespoke equipment is required.

threats.name: Cloud/App Credential Spoofing
threats.description: An attacker impersonates a legitimate user by obtaining valid credentials (passwords, PINs, or static tokens), allowing unauthorized access to remote services.

elapsedTime.rationale: Once credentials are obtained, logging in as the legitimate user takes minutes.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Using a stolen static password or token requires no more than basic scripting or tooling proficiency.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The targeted login flow is the same public-facing app or portal used by legitimate customers; no non-public OEM backend information is required.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: OEM cloud/app login endpoints are continuously reachable from the internet.

equipment.rationale: A browser or basic HTTP client is sufficient to replay stolen credentials.

threats.name: Malicious Firmware Update Deployment
threats.description: An attacker distributes and successfully installs tampered or unauthorized firmware packages by spoofing the backend or bypassing digital signature verifications.

elapsedTime.rationale: Bypassing OEM signing infrastructure or extracting backend signing keys is a sustained, multi-month research effort.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires expert knowledge to bypass OEM signing structures or hardware roots of trust.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires proprietary knowledge of the OEM's specific signing/verification chain and update packaging format.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The OTA/update channel and backend signing infrastructure are both persistently reachable; no narrow physical timing window is required.

equipment.rationale: Requires specialized reverse engineering or glitching equipment.

threats.name: Counterfeit or Rogue Hardware Integration
threats.description: Exploitation of the supply chain or physical vehicle access to insert counterfeit or malicious hardware components that successfully bypass component authentication.

elapsedTime.rationale: Designing, fabricating, and integrating counterfeit hardware that passes component authentication requires sustained supply-chain or hardware engineering effort.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine hardware and firmware engineering expertise to replicate authentication behavior.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires confidential schematic or layout knowledge to successfully bypass hardware authentication.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires physical access to the vehicle internals or supply chain interdiction.

equipment.rationale: Standard PCB rework and programming tools are sufficient for supply-chain insertion; no bespoke fabrication line is required.

threats.name: Backend and Mobile App Spoofing
threats.description: An attacker who has obtained backend or companion-app authentication material (e.g., stolen API keys or a forged TLS certificate) impersonates the OEM backend or mobile app to inject unauthorized commands into the vehicle over the telematics channel - distinct from T.01.2, which requires stealing an individual user's own login credentials.

elapsedTime.rationale: Extracting backend or mobile-app API keys/tokens via reverse engineering or endpoint abuse takes days to weeks.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine reverse-engineering or API-security expertise to extract and replay the forged credential material.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The mobile app and backend API surface are analyzable via standard reverse-engineering; no OEM-internal documentation is needed.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Always available remotely if the vehicle has cellular coverage.

equipment.rationale: A laptop, decompiler, and HTTP proxy are sufficient.

threats.name: In-Vehicle Network (IVN) Spoofing
threats.description: An attacker with access to the internal vehicle network generates or modifies messages to impersonate legitimate ECUs, bypassing internal trust boundaries.

elapsedTime.rationale: Reverse-engineering the target ECU's message IDs and signals and crafting spoofed frames takes days to weeks of bus analysis.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate embedded-systems and protocol-analysis skill to interpret bus traffic and craft valid frames.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific, largely non-public CAN/LIN/FlexRay message ID mapping and signal encoding used by the target OEM.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires physical or already-compromised access to the internal bus segment, not available from outside the vehicle.

equipment.rationale: A commodity CAN/automotive-Ethernet interface (e.g., USB-CAN adapter) is sufficient.

threats.name: GNSS/Location Spoofing
threats.description: An attacker manipulates or falsifies the vehicle's reported location by generating stronger, counterfeit GNSS RF signals.

elapsedTime.rationale: Overpowering a genuine GNSS signal with a stronger counterfeit signal takes minutes once the SDR is configured.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Turnkey GNSS spoofing toolchains (e.g., gps-sdr-sim) require only basic operating proficiency.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Civilian GNSS signal structure is a fully public, unencrypted standard; no vehicle- or OEM-specific knowledge is needed.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires only that the spoofing signal be stronger than the genuine satellite signal at the target's antenna, an easily achievable local condition.

equipment.rationale: Requires SDR (Software Defined Radio) equipment which is highly accessible.

threats.name: ADAS Perception Spoofing
threats.description: An attacker projects false physical signals to trick the ADAS perception layer into detecting phantom objects or ignoring real ones.

elapsedTime.rationale: Crafting a physical or projected spoofing pattern effective against a specific sensor fusion pipeline takes days to weeks of trial and testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine signal-processing or optics expertise to defeat sensor fusion, though not full adversarial-ML model access.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires understanding of the specific sensor fusion logic to create effective adversarial inputs.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Line-of-sight to the target vehicle's sensors during operation is a readily obtainable window (roadside placement, drone projection).

equipment.rationale: Requires specialized optical or EM projection hardware.

threats.name: Message Replay Attack
threats.description: Capturing valid network transmissions and retransmitting them later to trick the system into performing an unauthorized action.

elapsedTime.rationale: Capturing and retransmitting a valid frame is a near-instantaneous scripted operation.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Off-the-shelf capture/replay tools require only basic operating proficiency.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires only observing traffic on the bus, not confidential knowledge of message semantics, unless a freshness counter must also be bypassed.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires access to the bus to capture and later inject frames, an easily obtainable window once initial bus access exists.

equipment.rationale: A commodity CAN/Ethernet interface capable of capture-and-replay is sufficient.

threats.name: Diagnostic Credential Spoofing
threats.description: An attacker impersonates a technician by obtaining valid credentials (seeds, passwords), allowing unauthorized access to vehicle diagnostic functions.

elapsedTime.rationale: Recovering a short or static UDS seed-key secret or replaying stolen technician credentials is quick once bus access exists.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic scripting against a known or weak seed-key algorithm requires only proficient-level skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Many OEM seed-key algorithms are weak or have leaked publicly via aftermarket tool reverse engineering, keeping this restricted rather than sensitive.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Diagnostic access via OBD-II is readily available once physical or remote diagnostic connectivity exists.

equipment.rationale: A commodity UDS/diagnostic pass-through tool is sufficient.

threats.name: V2X Safety Message Injection
threats.description: An attacker broadcasts forged V2X Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM) or Decentralized Environmental Notification Messages (DENM), spoofing phantom vehicles or false hazard conditions to manipulate ADAS decision logic or mislead the driver.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forging and broadcasting a CAM/DENM message is fast once a V2X radio and certificate are available, but obtaining a usable pseudonym certificate or defeating misbehavior detection takes some preparation.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires working knowledge of the V2X message format and security profile (IEEE 1609.2) and RF broadcast, more than basic scripting.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: V2X message formats (ETSI ITS) are public standards.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires proximity (DSRC ~300 m) or a rogue V2X RSU.

equipment.rationale: Requires a V2X-capable radio and a valid or forged pseudonym certificate.

threats.name: EV Charging Session Spoofing
threats.description: An attacker deploys a rogue or tampered EVSE that presents a forged TLS certificate during the ISO 15118 Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) handshake. Upon a successful TLS downgrade or certificate validation bypass, the attacker can extract the vehicle's contract certificate, manipulate AC/DC charging parameters, or deliver a malicious firmware payload via the update channel.

elapsedTime.rationale: Building a rogue EVSE controller and reliably forcing a TLS downgrade or certificate-validation bypass across the ISO 15118 handshake takes months of protocol engineering.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine embedded and TLS protocol expertise to build a rogue EVSE and manipulate the V2G handshake.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: ISO 15118 is a public standard but OEM-specific certificate chains require research.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires physical access to a charging session (public charger swap or rogue station).

equipment.rationale: Requires a custom EVSE controller or a modified charging station.

threats.name: Cryptographic/Transport Protocol Downgrade Attack
threats.description: An attacker positioned as a man-in-the-middle actively manipulates a TLS/DTLS (or equivalent transport-security) handshake - stripping supported cipher suites from the ClientHello, forcing fallback to a deprecated protocol version (SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1), or exploiting cross-protocol/export-grade cryptographic weaknesses in the POODLE, FREAK, Logjam, or DROWN family - to coerce both endpoints into negotiating a version or cipher suite weak enough to break or cryptanalyze. Unlike the RF/PHY jamming-based downgrade modeled in T.08.3 (which forces a wireless interface to fail over from 4G/5G or WPA3 to 2G or WEP), this is a pure protocol-layer manipulation that requires no signal disruption at all, and it applies uniformly to any TLS/DTLS-secured channel in the vehicle's architecture: backend telematics sessions, OTA update distribution, and the ISO 15118 V2G/EVSE charging handshake.

elapsedTime.rationale: A MITM position combined with scripted handshake manipulation can force a downgrade within a single connection attempt; locating a still-viable weak-cipher fallback path on a well-maintained target takes longer reconnaissance.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires working knowledge of TLS/DTLS handshake internals and the specific cross-protocol cryptanalytic weakness being exploited (e.g., export-grade RSA factoring, SSLv2 Bleichenbacher oracle), not just generic packet interception.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires reconnaissance of which legacy protocol versions and cipher suites the specific target endpoint (backend API, OTA server, or EVSE) still accepts.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires an established on-path or on-path-capable MITM position - a compromised Wi-Fi access point, a rogue EVSE, or a backend network vantage point - held for the duration of the handshake.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with widely available MITM proxy tooling (mitmproxy, sslstrip derivatives, testssl.sh) run from a laptop; no specialized hardware is required.

threats.notes: Generalizes the downgrade pattern beyond the RF/PHY jamming scope of T.08.3 (Downgrade to Insecure Protocols) and beyond the ISO 15118-specific mention in T.01.12 (EV Charging Session Spoofing); this entry models the reusable protocol-layer MITM downgrade mechanism itself, applicable to any TLS/DTLS-secured channel.

threats.name: LLM/Conversational AI Prompt Injection
threats.description: An attacker embeds malicious natural-language instructions in content the in-cabin LLM copilot (A.073) will ingest while forming a response - a webpage returned by a web search the assistant performs on the user's behalf, a calendar invite, a received message, a navigation POI description, or a crafted voice command spoken within microphone range - causing the assistant to execute an unintended, attacker-directed vehicle function (unlocking doors, sending a message, changing climate/navigation settings, or exfiltrating conversation history) while appearing to the user as ordinary assistant behavior. This is indirect prompt injection per OWASP's LLM01:2025 (ranked the #1 risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications). Unlike the catalog's other Inject-action threats, which manipulate a fixed-grammar protocol or API surface (a malformed CAN frame, a forged API call) to trigger a parsing, authentication, or logic flaw, here the 'injection' is semantic: plain natural-language text that exploits the LLM's inability to reliably distinguish trusted user intent from untrusted ingested content sharing the same context window. No malformed message, protocol violation, or memory-corruption primitive is involved - the attack succeeds entirely within the model's normal, correctly functioning natural-language reasoning.

elapsedTime.rationale: Embedding hidden or disguised instructions in a webpage, calendar invite, or message is near-instantaneous once the attacker knows the assistant will ingest that content type; no iterative exploit-chain construction is required.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Crafting an effective injection payload draws on prompt-engineering skill that is widely documented and practiced; no reverse engineering, cryptography, or memory-safety exploitation is needed.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Reliably bypassing a specific OEM's system-prompt guardrails and tool-calling permission boundaries requires reconnaissance of that assistant's specific behavior - which content sources it ingests and which functions it is willing to call - information that is not publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The poisoned content (a webpage, calendar invite, or message) can sit dormant indefinitely until the user's own query causes the assistant to retrieve and ingest it; no narrow timing window is required from the attacker.

equipment.rationale: Publishing a webpage, sending a calendar invite or message, or speaking a voice command requires no specialized hardware or software beyond what is already available to any user.

threats.notes: Distinct from the catalog's other Inject-action threats (e.g. T.01.11 V2X message injection, T.02.4 Runtime Code/Command Injection), which manipulate a fixed-grammar protocol or API surface to trigger a parsing, authentication, or memory-safety flaw. Here the payload is unstructured natural language and the vulnerability exploited is the LLM's own reasoning process - there is no malformed message or broken parser to point to. Applies specifically to A.073 (In-Cabin Conversational AI / LLM Copilot Interface); prior to this asset's addition, no catalog entry modeled an in-cabin system with tool-calling access to vehicle functions driven by unstructured natural-language input. UN R155 Annex 5 predates this threat class; no confident primary-source mapping was found, so unitedNationsRegulation155 is left empty rather than guessed. Citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection (https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/).

threats.name: V2X Sybil Attack / Multi-Identity Misbehavior
threats.description: An attacker holds or synthesizes multiple simultaneously-valid V2X pseudonym identities - rather than forging a single message under one identity, as modeled in T.01.11 (V2X Safety Message Injection) - to simulate the presence of many phantom vehicles, artificially inflate perceived traffic density, or synthesize a coordinated false hazard/collision-warning consensus that appears to originate from several independent, legitimately-signed senders at once. Plausibility checks and anomaly filters that evaluate each received message or sender identity in isolation for physical implausibility (e.g. a single vehicle reporting an impossible speed) are defeated by this coordinated multi-identity pattern, since no single message or identity is individually implausible - the inconsistency only emerges when correlating the population of concurrently-active identities against physical and behavioral constraints. Distinct from T.01.11 by the additional prerequisite of controlling or synthesizing multiple concurrent identities, not merely broadcasting one forged message.

elapsedTime.rationale: Obtaining or deriving several concurrently-valid pseudonym certificates - whether by compromising multiple onboard units, exploiting the certificate issuance/rotation policy, or key extraction across several devices - takes sustained effort measured in weeks to months, well beyond the single-session effort needed to forge one message under one identity (T.01.11).

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires working knowledge of the V2X message format and RF broadcast (as in T.01.11) plus an understanding of the target PKI's specific pseudonym-certificate issuance and rotation model (SCMS/CCMS) needed to hold or synthesize multiple concurrently-valid identities without an obvious policy violation.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: While the V2X message format itself is public (as in T.01.11), reliably fabricating a physically-plausible multi-identity pattern that evades correlation-based plausibility checks requires knowledge of the target region's specific pseudonym-rotation cadence and certificate-issuance policy, which is not public.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires proximity (DSRC/C-V2X range) or a rogue V2X RSU, identical to T.01.11.

equipment.rationale: Broadcasting several concurrent, mutually-consistent identities requires either multiple V2X radio front-ends or a software-defined radio platform capable of modeling several physically-consistent fabricated trajectories simultaneously - more capable equipment than the single V2X radio T.01.11 requires.

threats.notes: Refines the same parent (T.01) as T.01.11 but models a mechanistically distinct prerequisite: holding or synthesizing multiple concurrently-valid identities (Extract:Crypto:External), not merely broadcasting one forged message. Directly denied by C.21.1 (V2X Misbehavior Detection), which correlates the message stream across identities rather than validating each message's signature in isolation - the gap C.21's pseudonym-certificate authentication alone does not close. Citation: "Creating a realistic sybil attack dataset for inter-vehicle communication", Peer-to-Peer Networking and Applications (2025), https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12083-025-02058-w.

threats.name: Rogue V2X / Short-Range Radio Transmitter
threats.description: An attacker operates a software-defined radio or a modified V2X on-board unit within radio range of the vehicle and transmits crafted V2X, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth frames. This gives the attacker a two-way radio channel to the vehicle's external interfaces and lets malformed frames reach the parsers of the V2X / telematics module.

elapsedTime.rationale: Building and tuning an SDR transmitter for V2X or short-range radio takes days to a week.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Open-source SDR tooling and published V2X stacks require proficient, not expert, skills.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: V2X, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth formats are public standards.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The attacker must stay within radio range (tens to hundreds of metres) while the vehicle passes or is parked.

equipment.rationale: A commodity SDR or a second-hand V2X unit is enough.

threats.name: Tampering
threats.description: Unauthorized modification of data, code, or hardware within the vehicle system. This is the abstract base class for all tampering and integrity-based threats.

elapsedTime.rationale: Umbrella rating derived from this category's own children: the lowest-bar (easiest-for-attacker) elapsed time value found among them is ET1, from T.02.2 (Persistent Storage and Configuration/Calibration Tampering) - the most accessible instantiation of this abstract tactic along this dimension.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Umbrella rating derived from this category's own children: the lowest-bar (easiest-for-attacker) specialist expertise value found among them is SE1, from T.02.2 (Persistent Storage and Configuration/Calibration Tampering) - the most accessible instantiation of this abstract tactic along this dimension.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Umbrella rating derived from this category's own children: the lowest-bar (easiest-for-attacker) knowledge of the item/component value found among them is KoIC1, from T.02.4 (Runtime Code/Command Injection) - the most accessible instantiation of this abstract tactic along this dimension.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Umbrella rating derived from this category's own children: the lowest-bar (easiest-for-attacker) window of opportunity value found among them is WoO1, from T.02.1 (Runtime Memory/State Tampering) - the most accessible instantiation of this abstract tactic along this dimension.

equipment.rationale: Umbrella rating derived from this category's own children: the lowest-bar (easiest-for-attacker) equipment value found among them is Eq0, from T.02.1 (Runtime Memory/State Tampering) - the most accessible instantiation of this abstract tactic along this dimension.

threats.name: Runtime Memory/State Tampering
threats.description: Altering variables, system state, or code while it is actively being processed by the ECU in RAM, bypassing static storage protections (e.g., via buffer overflows).

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding and reliably triggering a memory-corruption primitive (buffer overflow, race condition) takes days to weeks of fuzzing and analysis.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine exploit-development skill (memory layout, ASLR/DEP bypass) beyond basic scripting.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific process's memory layout and mitigations in place, which is not publicly documented per-ECU.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once code-execution access exists, the runtime memory space is continuously available to attack.

equipment.rationale: Standard debugging/fuzzing software on a commodity PC is sufficient; no special hardware is needed.

threats.name: Persistent Storage and Configuration/Calibration Tampering
threats.description: Unauthorized logical modification of at-rest configuration files, calibration parameters (e.g., ADAS sensor limits, engine torque curves), routing tables, or OS files stored in NVRAM/EEPROM. Allows an attacker to alter vehicle behavior without needing to exploit or rewrite the actual executable firmware.

elapsedTime.rationale: Changing a config value is much faster than reverse-engineering and patching firmware.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Editing a known configuration or calibration file format requires only basic scripting skill once access exists.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowing the specific calibration formats or file paths.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Configuration/calibration storage is accessible for modification whenever write access to the ECU exists, with no narrow timing requirement.

equipment.rationale: Standard diagnostic or file-system tools suffice; no specialized equipment is required.

threats.name: Static Code Alteration
threats.description: Replacing or modifying the actual software/firmware executables stored on the device. Typically defended by Secure Boot and DM-Verity.

elapsedTime.rationale: Defeating Secure Boot/DM-Verity signature verification to persistently replace firmware requires months of reverse-engineering and exploit development.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Bypassing hardware-backed trust chains like Secure Boot requires advanced exploitation.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires understanding of the target's specific boot-chain and signing scheme, which is not publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires either sustained physical flashing access or a live elevation exploit; not available at will.

equipment.rationale: Software-only reverse-engineering and flashing tools suffice for the elevation-exploit path; no specialized lab hardware is required.

threats.name: Runtime Code/Command Injection
threats.description: Introducing malicious code or unauthorized system commands into a running application by exploiting input validation flaws (e.g., API payloads, malicious diagnostic requests).

elapsedTime.rationale: Discovering and reliably exploiting an input-validation flaw in an API or diagnostic handler takes days to weeks.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine application-security and fuzzing expertise to craft a working injection payload.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Exploitable input-validation flaws are typically found through black-box testing of the public-facing API/protocol surface, not confidential documentation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The vulnerable interface is available whenever the application or diagnostic service is running, an easily obtainable window.

equipment.rationale: Standard scripting/fuzzing tools on a commodity PC are sufficient.

threats.name: Hardware Fault Injection (Glitching)
threats.description: Deliberately introducing faults (voltage drops, clock manipulation, EM pulses) to disrupt normal SoC execution, allowing an attacker to skip security checks like Secure Boot or Authentication loops.

elapsedTime.rationale: Characterizing the target's exact glitch timing window (voltage, clock, or EM) requires months of iterative trial-and-error.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires combined expertise in power electronics, precise timing, and the target's boot-sequence internals.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the SoC's boot sequence and approximate check timing, which is reverse-engineered rather than publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires extended, unobserved physical access to the target board to characterize and repeat the glitch.

equipment.rationale: Requires oscilloscopes, precise timing trigger boards, and modified power supplies.

threats.name: Network Protocol Manipulation / Fuzzing
threats.description: Exploitation of in-vehicle communication protocols (CAN, Ethernet, UDS) by sending malformed or out-of-spec messages to induce crashes, overflow buffers, or force fallback states.

elapsedTime.rationale: Fuzzing a protocol stack until a crash or exploitable state is found typically takes days to weeks of automated testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate protocol-fuzzing and crash-triage skill to turn a malformed message into a usable effect.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: CAN/Ethernet/UDS protocol structures are publicly documented standards; only OEM-specific message content is non-public.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once network access is available, the protocol stack is continuously fuzzable with no narrow timing window.

equipment.rationale: A commodity CAN/Ethernet interface capable of malformed-frame injection is sufficient.

threats.name: Basic Physical Data Tampering (Exposed Pins)
threats.description: Gaining physical access to the ECU's PCB to directly modify memory chips utilizing exposed-pin architectures (TSOP, QFP, DIP), requiring significantly lower technical capabilities than hidden-pad packages.

elapsedTime.rationale: Locating exposed pins and rewriting the memory chip's contents takes hours to days of bench work.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate hardware and soldering skill and familiarity with the memory device's programming protocol.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific chip's pinout and the ECU's memory map.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires extended, unobserved physical possession of the removed or benched ECU board.

equipment.rationale: Standard soldering iron, hot air gun, and basic micro-probes are sufficient.

threats.notes: Requires physical possession of the target hardware (see T.06.6, Physical ECU / Vehicle Access) - modeled as an independent Root Attack Step rather than a formal capability prerequisite, since no capability in this taxonomy exclusively represents physical possession without being reachable through this catalog's dense software-privilege capability graph as well.

threats.name: Advanced Physical Data Tampering (Hidden Pads)
threats.description: Gaining physical access to the ECU's PCB to directly modify or rewrite memory chips utilizing hidden-pad architectures (BGA, LGA, WSON), bypassing software-level protections.

elapsedTime.rationale: BGA/LGA rework, decapsulation, and rewriting without destroying the die takes days to weeks per attempt, and often multiple attempts.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires advanced soldering and reballing expertise to avoid destroying the IC.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific package's ball/pad map, which is not publicly documented for most automotive-grade parts.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires extended, unobserved physical possession of the removed ECU board for rework.

equipment.rationale: Requires BGA rework stations, decapsulation chemicals, or X-ray inspection tools.

threats.notes: Requires physical possession of the target hardware (see T.06.6, Physical ECU / Vehicle Access) - modeled as an independent Root Attack Step rather than a formal capability prerequisite, since no capability in this taxonomy exclusively represents physical possession without being reachable through this catalog's dense software-privilege capability graph as well.

threats.name: Remote Code Execution via Telematics/IVI Interface
threats.description: An attacker exploits an unpatched vulnerability in the vehicle's external wireless stack (Bluetooth BLE, Wi-Fi 802.11, or cellular modem firmware) to gain initial unauthenticated code execution on the Telematics Control Unit (TCU) or IVI head unit without any prior vehicle access.

elapsedTime.rationale: Full wireless-stack exploit chains (BLE heap spray, Wi-Fi/cellular baseband RCE) take months of vulnerability research to develop reliably.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires full wireless stack exploit development (e.g., heap spray over BLE).

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires reverse-engineered knowledge of the specific modem/BLE-stack firmware version's vulnerabilities, not publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Wi-Fi/BLE requires proximity; cellular is always reachable while the vehicle has coverage.

equipment.rationale: Commodity SDR and a Linux laptop are sufficient.

threats.name: Firmware/Software Version Rollback (Downgrade) Attack
threats.description: An attacker reflashes or restores an ECU to an older, genuinely OEM-signed firmware or software image that contains a since-patched vulnerability, or directly tampers with the stored version value/rollback counter used to gate installation, without ever forging a signature. Because the replayed image carries a valid signature, Secure Boot's verification step passes without incident - the attack succeeds not by breaking cryptographic trust but by replaying a legitimately trusted artifact that predates a security fix. In the absence of monotonic anti-rollback enforcement (a hardware counter, blown eFuse, or software rollback-index comparison), the reintroduced, previously-patched vulnerability becomes available again for exploitation by a subsequent, independent attack.

elapsedTime.rationale: Sourcing or retaining a prior signed image and reflashing it, or overwriting a stored rollback counter, is a short, scriptable operation once write access is available.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires understanding of the target's specific versioning scheme - where the rollback counter is stored and checked, and any TOCTOU window between verification and load - but no cryptographic break is needed.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the ECU's prior firmware release history and of exactly how and where the version or rollback-index value is validated and stored.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires either physical/diagnostic flashing access to the target ECU or the ability to inject a malicious 'update' package via the OTA delivery channel.

equipment.rationale: A commodity diagnostic flasher or an OTA man-in-the-middle proxy is sufficient; no specialized laboratory equipment is required.

threats.notes: Threat-side counterpart to C.16.4 (Anti-Rollback Protection) and C.19.1 (Monotonic Counters), both of which mitigate exactly this mechanism. The standard defensive pattern this attack targets is the Android AVB Rollback Index model (monotonic per-partition rollback counters in tamper-evident storage).

threats.name: Certificate and Trust Store Tampering
threats.description: Unauthorized change of the certificates, trusted root keys, or key allow-lists that a component checks against, stored in writable memory. Examples are adding an attacker root certificate to a TLS trust store, replacing the public key used to verify firmware signatures, or adding a key to the list accepted for diagnostic access. The cryptography itself is not broken. The attacker makes the component trust their keys and certificates instead.

elapsedTime.rationale: Adding or swapping a certificate or key is quick once write access to the store exists.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Needs to know how the target validates certificates and where it keeps them, which is more than editing a plain configuration file.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowing the trust store format and location, which differs per platform.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The store can be changed whenever privileged or remote-management access exists, with no narrow timing requirement.

equipment.rationale: Standard tools are enough; no specialized equipment is required.

threats.name: Repudiation
threats.description: An entity performs a malicious or unauthorized action and successfully denies having performed it. In an automotive context, this typically involves an attacker masking their tracks by deleting diagnostic logs, or a compromised node successfully denying the origin of a spoofed V2X/backend message. This is the abstract base class for Repudiation.

threats.name: Audit Log Tampering and Evasion
threats.description: An attacker modifies, deletes, or floods Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs), crash data recorders (EDR), or security audit logs to cover their tracks. This ensures the attack cannot be traced, analyzed by the SOC, or legally proven.

elapsedTime.rationale: Erasing or overwriting log entries once write access exists is a fast, scripted operation.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires only basic scripting once the log storage location is known.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowing where the logs are stored and the UDS routines to clear them.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Log storage is writable whenever elevated or network access to the ECU exists, an easily obtainable window.

equipment.rationale: Standard diagnostic or file-system tools suffice.

threats.name: Repudiation of Origin (V2X / Backend)
threats.description: A node transmits a malicious or malformed message (e.g., a fake V2X safety hazard warning or a rogue OTA command) and successfully denies sending it because the communication channel lacks sufficient non-repudiation controls, such as digital signatures binding the message to a single sender - a shared symmetric MAC alone cannot provide this guarantee, since any party holding the key could have produced it.

elapsedTime.rationale: Crafting a message that lacks attributable signing while still appearing plausible takes some preparation and testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires understanding of the channel's missing non-repudiation controls to exploit the gap deliberately.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The absence of message-level signing is often discoverable through protocol observation rather than confidential documentation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The channel is available for injection whenever network access exists.

equipment.rationale: Standard V2X radio or API client tooling is sufficient.

threats.name: Information Disclosure
threats.description: Unauthorized exposure of sensitive data, such as personal identifiable information (PII), cryptographic keys, IP, or system state. This is the abstract base class for all disclosure and confidentiality threats.

threats.name: In-Vehicle Network (IVN) Sniffing
threats.description: Passively capturing unencrypted data exchanged within the vehicle (e.g., CAN, LIN, or Automotive Ethernet traffic) to extract sensitive telemetry, user data, or reverse-engineer command structures.

elapsedTime.rationale: Passive capture begins the instant a sniffing tool is connected.

specialistExpertise.rationale: CAN sniffing tools are heavily commoditized.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: CAN/LIN/Ethernet frame formats are publicly documented; interpreting specific payloads may need some reverse engineering.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires physical access to the OBD-II port or an exposed IVN bus wire, or a compromised ECU.

equipment.rationale: A commodity CAN sniffer/USB-CAN adapter is sufficient.

threats.name: External Communications Interception
threats.description: An attacker positions themselves on the vehicle's external communication path (e.g., deploying a rogue Wi-Fi AP, cellular IMSI catcher, or BGP route injection) to intercept data transmitted between the vehicle and external entities. Allows the theft of credentials, session tokens, or PII.

elapsedTime.rationale: Deploying a rogue AP/IMSI catcher and capturing meaningful traffic takes days of positioning and monitoring.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate RF/networking expertise to configure interception infrastructure convincingly.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Wi-Fi/cellular/BLE protocols are public standards; only the specific pairing/session behavior is discovered through observation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires proximity for Wi-Fi/BLE positioning; carrier-level access for cellular (IMSI catcher).

equipment.rationale: Requires Wi-Fi/Bluetooth sniffers, rogue APs, or SDR base stations.

threats.name: Unintended Disclosure of PII Data
threats.description: Exposure of sensitive user data (location history, contacts, biometrics) due to misconfiguration, excessive debug logging, or insecure HMI implementations in the Infotainment/Telematics domains.

elapsedTime.rationale: Reading over-logged or misconfigured data once access exists is immediate.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Locating verbose debug logs or misconfigured storage requires only basic familiarity with the platform.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Debug log locations and formats are often discoverable through generic platform knowledge (e.g., Android logcat conventions), not confidential documentation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Exposed logs/interfaces are available whenever the corresponding access level is held.

equipment.rationale: No special equipment is required beyond standard access tools.

threats.name: Side Channel Analysis (SCA)
threats.description: Passively exploiting indirect physical leakage - timing variations, power consumption patterns, or electromagnetic emissions - observed during normal cryptographic processing to statistically recover secret key material without physical intervention in circuit operation.

elapsedTime.rationale: Collecting thousands of traces and performing statistical key-recovery analysis is a multi-month undertaking.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires advanced statistical signal processing (DPA/CPA/TVLA) to isolate key-correlated leakage from measurement noise across thousands of traces.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Knowledge of the cryptographic algorithm and approximate hardware layout is sufficient; exact gate-level implementation is not required.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires repeated physical proximity to the operating device to collect sufficient power/EM traces; not achievable from an unconstrained offline capture alone.

equipment.rationale: Requires high-frequency oscilloscopes (≥1 GSa/s), EM near-field probes, and low-noise amplifiers. Commercially available.

threats.name: Differential Fault Analysis (DFA)
threats.description: Actively inducing precise computational faults in a cryptographic operation - via voltage glitching, clock manipulation, electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI), or laser irradiation - then statistically analyzing the differential between correct and faulty ciphertext outputs to derive the secret key. Unlike SCA, DFA actively disturbs circuit operation rather than passively observing it.

elapsedTime.rationale: Characterizing exploitable fault windows and collecting sufficient faulty-ciphertext pairs for differential analysis takes months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires simultaneous expertise in fault injection hardware, cryptographic differential analysis, and precise timing of fault windows within the cryptographic round schedule.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Exact knowledge of the cryptographic implementation's round timing and target register layout is required to position the fault within the exploitable window.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires extended, unobserved physical access to induce and repeat precisely-timed faults against the operating device.

equipment.rationale: Requires precision fault injection platforms (laser FI workstation, EMFI pulse generators, sub-nanosecond timing controllers). Significantly more specialized than SCA equipment.

threats.name: Advanced Physical Data Extraction (Hidden Pads)
threats.description: Directly reading data from storage devices or memory chips utilizing hidden-pad architectures (BGA, LGA, WSON) using physical access techniques like X-ray alignment, chip-off, or decapsulation to extract firmware and keys.

elapsedTime.rationale: Decapsulation/chip-off extraction from BGA/LGA/WSON packages without destroying the die takes days to weeks per attempt.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires combined expertise in advanced hardware rework, X-ray alignment, and forensic data recovery.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific package's pad layout, not publicly documented for most automotive parts.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires extended, unobserved physical possession of the extracted board or chip.

equipment.rationale: Requires X-ray alignment systems, decapsulation chemicals, or chip-off rework stations.

threats.notes: Requires physical possession of the target hardware (see T.06.6, Physical ECU / Vehicle Access) - modeled as an independent Root Attack Step rather than a formal capability prerequisite, since no capability in this taxonomy exclusively represents physical possession without being reachable through this catalog's dense software-privilege capability graph as well.

threats.name: Basic Physical Data Extraction (Exposed Pins)
threats.description: Directly reading data from memory chips utilizing exposed-pin architectures (TSOP, QFP, DIP) using standard in-circuit clips or basic desoldering to extract firmware. Requires significantly less effort than BGA extraction.

elapsedTime.rationale: Attaching test clips and dumping an exposed-pin memory chip takes hours.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate hardware skill to identify pinout and operate a programmer or logic analyzer.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific chip's pinout and the ECU's memory map.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires extended, unobserved physical possession of the board.

equipment.rationale: Standard test clips, logic analyzers, and basic soldering gear are sufficient.

threats.notes: Requires physical possession of the target hardware (see T.06.6, Physical ECU / Vehicle Access) - modeled as an independent Root Attack Step rather than a formal capability prerequisite, since no capability in this taxonomy exclusively represents physical possession without being reachable through this catalog's dense software-privilege capability graph as well.

threats.name: OEM Backend Credential / Key Extraction
threats.description: An attacker compromises the OEM's cloud backend through web-application vulnerabilities (SQL injection, insecure object references, credential stuffing against the DevOps pipeline) or insider access to extract cryptographic signing keys, OTA authorization tokens, or fleet-wide symmetric secrets from the backend key management service.

elapsedTime.rationale: Discovering and successfully exploiting a web-application vulnerability or insider vector in a production OEM backend takes months of reconnaissance and testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine web-application security or insider-access expertise, not basic scripting.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Public API endpoints and OEM web portals are observable.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Backend is always reachable from the internet.

equipment.rationale: Standard web-application testing tools (proxy, scanner) are sufficient.

threats.name: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL)
threats.description: A long-horizon quantum threat strategy in which an attacker passively intercepts and stores encrypted vehicle communications today - over V2X, TLS/DTLS-protected telematics channels, or OEM backend links - with the intent of retroactively decrypting them once a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) becomes available. Shor's algorithm enables a CRQC to break classical asymmetric key exchange (RSA, ECDH, ECDSA), rendering all previously captured ciphertext retroactively readable. Beyond confidentiality, HNDL enables 'harvest now, spoof later': stored public-key material allows a quantum-capable attacker to derive corresponding private signing keys, subsequently forging digital signatures on OTA packages, V2X messages, or backend API tokens - enabling injection of malicious commands or unauthorized firmware execution.

elapsedTime.rationale: The 'harvest' phase is immediate and passive; the 'decrypt later' phase requires years of CRQC development. Nation-state adversaries are already executing collection operations against automotive and V2X traffic with long-term decryption intent.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Passive traffic interception is trivial; retroactive decryption and private-key derivation via Shor's algorithm requires advanced quantum computing expertise and CRQC access.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Classical asymmetric protocols (RSA, ECDH, ECDSA) used in TLS/DTLS, V2X (IEEE 1609.2), and OTA are publicly standardized; their vulnerability to Shor's algorithm is well-documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Passive interception requires only brief or opportunistic positioning on a communication path; the decryption phase is performed offline at a future time.

equipment.rationale: Requires a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC). Not yet commercially available, but nation-state actors are actively investing in CRQC development and the risk window is within automotive vehicle lifetime horizons (10–15 years).

threats.description: Disrupting the normal operation of vehicle systems by overwhelming resources, blocking communications, or causing system crashes. This is the abstract base class for all availability threats.

elapsedTime.rationale: Umbrella rating derived from this category's own children: the lowest-bar (easiest-for-attacker) elapsed time value found among them is ET1, from T.05.1 (In-Vehicle Network (IVN) Bus Flooding) - the most accessible instantiation of this abstract tactic along this dimension.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Umbrella rating derived from this category's own children: the lowest-bar (easiest-for-attacker) specialist expertise value found among them is SE0, from T.05.3 (Wireless RF / GNSS Jamming) - the most accessible instantiation of this abstract tactic along this dimension.

threats.name: In-Vehicle Network (IVN) Bus Flooding
threats.description: Injecting excessive high-priority messages (e.g., CAN frame ID 0x000 flooding, Ethernet broadcast storms) to consume available bandwidth, preventing legitimate safety-critical messages from arriving at their destination.

elapsedTime.rationale: Flooding begins immediately once network access is available.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Simple scripts or off-the-shelf CAN tools can generate bus floods.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: CAN arbitration/priority behavior is public knowledge; only the target bus's specific ID assignments may need minor reconnaissance.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires physical access to OBD-II or an exposed network wire.

equipment.rationale: A commodity CAN interface capable of high-rate frame injection is sufficient.

threats.name: Compute Resource Exhaustion
threats.description: Intentionally consuming excessive system resources on an ECU (CPU cycles, RAM, file descriptors) by exploiting logic flaws, infinite loops, or sending complex continuous inputs, forcing the OS to hang or crash.

elapsedTime.rationale: Identifying a resource-exhaustion logic flaw or crafting a suitably complex input takes days of testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate understanding of the target application's resource-handling logic.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Common resource-exhaustion patterns (infinite loops, unbounded allocation) are general software-engineering knowledge, not OEM-specific.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once execution access is available, the resource-exhaustion trigger can be attempted repeatedly with no narrow timing window.

equipment.rationale: No special equipment beyond the existing execution access is required.

threats.name: Wireless RF / GNSS Jamming
threats.description: Emitting powerful RF noise to interfere with and block the vehicle's wireless reception, disabling location-based services (GNSS), cellular telematics, Bluetooth key fobs, or V2X safety communications.

elapsedTime.rationale: Overwhelming the target receiver with RF noise produces a disruptive effect within seconds of transmission.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Jamming requires zero expertise; turn the device on and it works.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: RF jamming exploits the physics of the shared spectrum and requires no vehicle- or OEM-specific knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Attacker must be in physical proximity to the vehicle.

equipment.rationale: GPS/Cellular jammers are cheap and widely available online.

threats.name: Denial of Wallet (Cloud API Exhaustion)
threats.description: An attacker targets the OEM's backend infrastructure by generating massive amounts of automated API requests (e.g., querying vehicle status, requesting OTA updates). This forces the cloud infrastructure to auto-scale, incurring massive financial costs for the OEM.

elapsedTime.rationale: Scripting a high-volume automated request flood is fast to set up.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic scripting against a public API endpoint is sufficient.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Public REST/MQTT API endpoints are documented for legitimate app integration and require no confidential OEM information to abuse at volume.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Public APIs are always available.

equipment.rationale: Commodity load-testing/scripting tools are sufficient.

threats.name: Denial of Service via Logical Deletion (Bricking)
threats.description: An attacker intentionally deletes critical system files, boot configurations, routing tables, or cryptographic keys from persistent storage. This renders the ECU or vehicle network locally inoperable, resulting in a permanent or semi-permanent denial of service without requiring continuous network flooding.

elapsedTime.rationale: Deleting critical files or keys once write access exists is near-instantaneous.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires only basic file-system/flash operations once access is available.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowing which files/partitions are critical to boot, information that is reverse-engineerable rather than confidential.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Persistent storage is writable whenever elevated or network access is held, with no narrow timing constraint.

equipment.rationale: Standard diagnostic or file-system tools suffice.

threats.name: CAN Bus-Off / Error-State Forced Disconnection Attack
threats.description: An attacker exploits the CAN controller's built-in error-confinement state machine rather than raw bandwidth exhaustion. By injecting frames sharing the same arbitration ID as a victim ECU's next scheduled transmission and forcing a bit-level conflict (or corrupting the victim's own frame with a jammed dominant bit at the right moment), the attacker repeatedly drives transmit-error-counter (TEC) increments on the victim's CAN controller. Once the TEC exceeds 255, the controller autonomously transitions to the 'bus-off' state per the CAN/ISO 11898-1 error-handling specification and physically disconnects itself from the bus - silently and durably removing a legitimate, uncompromised ECU from the network without transmitting a single flooded frame, and typically without the victim ECU's own software ever detecting the transition.

elapsedTime.rationale: Driving enough consecutive TEC increments across the 255-count bus-off threshold on a specific targeted ID takes tens to low hundreds of milliseconds of precisely timed injection - longer than an instantaneous flood, but still well within a single attack session.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires understanding of the CAN error-confinement state machine (error-active/error-passive/bus-off transitions and TEC/REC counting rules), which is materially more specialized than simple frame injection.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the victim ECU's specific arbitration ID and transmission schedule to reliably win repeated arbitration collisions against it.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires direct electrical access to the target CAN segment - via OBD-II, an exposed harness splice, or a already-compromised ECU bridging onto the segment.

equipment.rationale: A commodity CAN transceiver/interface capable of sub-millisecond frame timing (e.g., a modified USB-CAN adapter) is sufficient; no specialized lab equipment is required.

threats.notes: Distinct from the flooding-based Denial of Service modeled in T.05.1 (IVN Bus Flooding) and T.20.4 (CAN Bus Denial of Service, Auto-ISAC ATM-T0068): this attack silently removes a single targeted ECU from the bus via the CAN error-confinement state machine rather than exhausting bus bandwidth, and can succeed with a small fraction of the frames a flood requires.

threats.name: Ransomware / Extortion Attack on Backend Infrastructure
threats.description: An attacker who has already gained code-execution access to OEM or fleet backend infrastructure (dealer-management systems, fleet-operations APIs, telematics backend) - for example via T.01.5 (Backend and Mobile App Spoofing) - deploys ransomware to encrypt backend data and systems, rendering fleet operations, OTA update distribution, and remote vehicle services unavailable. Before triggering encryption, the attacker exfiltrates sensitive data (customer PII, vehicle telemetry, proprietary fleet-operations data) to hold as 'double extortion' leverage, threatening public disclosure if the ransom is not paid even if the victim can restore from backup without paying. Distinct from T.05.5 (Denial of Service via Logical Deletion), which models destructive, non-recoverable deletion for its own sake: this threat's mechanism is recoverable-in-principle encryption paired with a parallel data-theft/extortion component, and its objective is financial extraction rather than pure sabotage.

elapsedTime.rationale: Once the code-execution foothold exists, deploying commodity ransomware-as-a-service tooling to encrypt backend data stores and stage exfiltration is achievable within days, given how automated modern ransomware affiliate toolkits are.

specialistExpertise.rationale: The affiliate deploying the ransomware payload needs only standard IT/network-administration skill; the harder exploit-development work needed to obtain the initial backend foothold is scored on the prerequisite threat (e.g. T.01.5), not here.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Maximizing both the disruption and extortion leverage requires reconnaissance of the specific backend's data topology - identifying which systems host fleet-operations, OTA distribution, and customer PII - which is not public information.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once a backend foothold exists, the attacker can move to encryption/exfiltration at a time of their choosing; the main constraint is avoiding detection before the payload completes, not a narrow external timing window.

equipment.rationale: Commodity ransomware-as-a-service toolkits, obtainable through dark-web affiliate programs, and standard IT administration tools are sufficient; no specialized equipment is required.

threats.notes: Upstream Security's 2026 Global Automotive and Smart Mobility Cybersecurity Report found ransomware-related incidents accounted for 44% of all reported automotive/smart-mobility cybersecurity incidents analyzed for 2025, roughly double the prior year's count. Chains from T.01.5 (Backend and Mobile App Spoofing), whose grants provide the Execute:Executable:Backend foothold this threat requires. Report: https://upstream.auto/reports/global-automotive-cybersecurity-report/.

threats.name: EV Charging Communication Disruption (Wireless PLC Jamming)
threats.description: An attacker wirelessly disrupts the HomePlug GreenPHY power-line-communication signaling between the vehicle's EV Communication Controller (A.069) and the charging station during the ISO 15118/DIN 70121 SLAC (Signal Level Attenuation Characterization) handshake or an active charging session. The attack exploits the CSMA/CA (carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance) behavior mandated by the HomePlug GreenPHY standard: transmitting a weak, precisely-timed RF signal that the receiving station's carrier-sense logic interprets as channel activity is sufficient to prevent legitimate session establishment or abort an in-progress charge, without any physical or electrical connection to the vehicle or charging station. Distinct from T.01.12 (EV Charging Session Spoofing, a confidentiality/integrity threat requiring a rogue EVSE and TLS manipulation) and T.01.13 (protocol downgrade, requiring an on-path MITM position): this is a pure availability/DoS threat, requiring no cryptographic capability, no rogue infrastructure, and no wired access - only modest RF equipment operated at range.

elapsedTime.rationale: Once positioned within range, disrupting the SLAC handshake or aborting an active session is achievable within seconds of transmitting, as demonstrated experimentally against real CCS charging equipment.

specialistExpertise.rationale: The published Brokenwire methodology and reference tooling make replication straightforward for anyone with basic RF/SDR familiarity; no novel protocol-break or cryptographic expertise is required.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The exploited carrier-sense behavior is a mandatory, publicly documented part of the HomePlug GreenPHY, DIN 70121, and ISO 15118 standards, not proprietary OEM-specific information.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires the attacker to be within RF range of the vehicle or charging station (demonstrated effective up to approximately 47 meters) during the handshake or an active session - a real but modest proximity constraint.

equipment.rationale: Demonstrated effective with a sub-1-watt, modestly modified software-defined radio or PLC transceiver; no specialized or expensive laboratory equipment is required.

threats.notes: Real-world precedent: the Brokenwire attack (University of Oxford / armasuisse S+T, NDSS 2023), demonstrated against real Combined Charging System (CCS) equipment at ranges up to ~47 m using under 1 W of transmit power, with implications for a substantial share of the roughly 12 million battery-electric vehicles on the road at time of disclosure. No requires capability is modeled, consistent with T.05.3 (Wireless RF / GNSS Jamming): this is a baseline RF-proximity attack that presupposes no prior compromise. Paper: Kohler, Baker, Strohmeier & Martinovic, "Brokenwire: Wireless Disruption of CCS Electric Vehicle Charging", NDSS Symposium 2023, https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2023-251-paper.pdf.

threats.name: OS / Kernel Privilege Escalation
threats.description: Exploiting local vulnerabilities (e.g., buffer overflows, race conditions, use-after-free) within the vehicle's Operating System or Kernel to transition from a restricted user space application to root or administrative access.

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding and reliably weaponizing a kernel-level memory-corruption vulnerability takes months of vulnerability research.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine kernel-exploitation expertise (race conditions, use-after-free, ROP chaining).

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific kernel build/version's memory layout and mitigations, not publicly documented per-ECU.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once user-space execution exists, the kernel attack surface is continuously available with no narrow timing window.

equipment.rationale: Standard exploit-development tooling on a commodity PC is sufficient.

threats.name: Hypervisor / TEE Breakout
threats.description: Gaining unauthorized processing capabilities by escaping standard execution environments (Normal World or Guest VM) to access highly protected hardware domains (Secure World, TEE, or Hypervisor root level) running crypto-operations or critical routing.

elapsedTime.rationale: Escaping a hardware-enforced hypervisor/TEE boundary is among the hardest classes of exploit, typically requiring 6+ months of dedicated research.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires extremely advanced exploit development and deep hardware architecture knowledge.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires deep, non-public knowledge of the specific hypervisor/TEE implementation's isolation boundaries.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once guest-level execution exists, the hypervisor attack surface is continuously available.

equipment.rationale: Purely software exploitation; no specialized hardware is required to attempt the breakout.

threats.name: Application / Container Sandbox Breakout
threats.description: Escaping application sandboxes (e.g., Android Automotive app permissions) or OCI containers (Docker) running on an HPC node. The attacker elevates from a restricted app context to full host OS access.

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding and chaining a sandbox-escape vulnerability in a container runtime or app framework takes days to weeks.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate exploit-development skill in the specific sandboxing technology (namespaces, seccomp, Android permissions).

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Container/Android sandboxing internals are publicly documented technologies; only the specific hardening configuration is non-public.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Often achievable remotely if an attacker compromises a connected infotainment app.

equipment.rationale: Purely software exploitation; no special equipment required.

threats.name: Exploitation of Open Debug Ports (JTAG/UART)
threats.description: Utilizing unprotected or improperly disabled hardware debug channels left open from the development phase to bypass software restrictions, drop into a root shell, or manually alter execution flow.

elapsedTime.rationale: Connecting to an open, unauthenticated debug port and dropping into a shell is nearly instantaneous.

specialistExpertise.rationale: JTAG/UART connection and shell interaction require only basic hardware-hacking proficiency.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Debug pinouts are frequently identifiable via public teardown/reverse-engineering resources for the same ECU family.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires physical access to the PCB headers.

equipment.rationale: A commodity JTAG/UART adapter and logic analyzer are sufficient.

threats.notes: Requires physical possession of the target hardware (see T.06.6, Physical ECU / Vehicle Access) - modeled as an independent Root Attack Step rather than a formal capability prerequisite, since no capability in this taxonomy exclusively represents physical possession without being reachable through this catalog's dense software-privilege capability graph as well.

threats.name: Elevation of Privilege via Misconfiguration
threats.description: An attacker leverages insecure system configurations, such as default engineering passwords, open Telnet/SSH ports, overly permissive file access controls (DAC), or forgotten debug flags left in production builds, to trivially gain administrative or root access to the system.

elapsedTime.rationale: Exploiting misconfigurations is often instantaneous compared to developing memory corruption exploits.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Can be executed by a layman using automated scanning tools or known default password lists.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Default credentials and open ports are often industry-wide knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Default credentials or open debug ports are available whenever the corresponding interface is reachable, an easily obtainable window.

equipment.rationale: Standard scanning tools and public default-credential lists are sufficient.

threats.name: Physical ECU / Vehicle Access
threats.description: An attacker gains physical access to vehicle internals (ECU PCB, wiring harness, or OBD-II port), enabling hardware-level attack primitives that cannot be achieved remotely. This is the foundational access condition that roots the physical-access attack chain.

elapsedTime.rationale: Gaining unobserved physical access to vehicle internals (removing panels, connecting to OBD-II) takes hours to days depending on the access scenario.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires only basic mechanical/technical proficiency to access vehicle internals.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: General ECU/harness locations are discoverable through public repair manuals and teardown videos; exact layouts vary by OEM.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires physical proximity and unobserved access time (e.g., a workshop, overnight parking, or supply chain access).

equipment.rationale: Basic tools (screwdrivers, OBD-II adapter, logic analyzer clips) are sufficient to gain initial physical access to ECU internals.

threats.name: Cross-Domain Lateral Movement
threats.description: An attacker with code execution in the Infotainment or Telematics domain exploits a misconfigured or unfiltered central gateway ECU to inject messages directly onto Powertrain-domain bus segments (e.g., CAN-FD) or escalate to host-OS access on an HPC node bridging both domains.

elapsedTime.rationale: Mapping and defeating the specific gateway's filtering rules from a foothold in Infotainment/Telematics takes months of reconnaissance.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires deep knowledge of OEM-specific gateway routing tables and firewall rules.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Gateway configuration is OEM-confidential.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once code execution exists in Telematics/Infotainment, the gateway interface is continuously reachable.

equipment.rationale: Purely software reconnaissance and message crafting; no special equipment required.

threats.name: Backend API Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA)
threats.description: An attacker who holds a valid but unprivileged session with the OEM's owner/companion-app or fleet-management backend API exploits a missing per-request ownership check - commonly an endpoint that trusts a client-supplied, enumerable identifier such as a VIN, dealer ID, or internal vehicle record ID without verifying it belongs to the calling account - to remotely issue unlock, remote-start, horn/light, or location-query commands against, or read PII belonging to, vehicles the attacker does not own. No credential theft, key extraction, or cryptographic bypass is required: the attacker's own account and session are fully legitimate, and the API itself performs the privileged action on the attacker's behalf against the wrong object. This is functionally distinct from T.01.2 (which requires stolen credentials belonging to another account) and from T.04.8 (where an IDOR-class flaw is used only to exfiltrate keys/secrets, not to directly execute commands against another owner's vehicle).

elapsedTime.rationale: Once a vulnerable endpoint is identified, iterating over VINs and replaying the unlock/start/locate request is near-instantaneous and fully scriptable.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires only standard web/API testing skills (intercepting proxy, parameter tampering) - no cryptography, reverse engineering, or hardware access is needed.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: VINs are printed on the vehicle itself (windshield, door jamb) and are structurally decodable/enumerable; no confidential OEM information is required to obtain one.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The backend API is continuously reachable over the internet from anywhere in the world; there is no operational time-window constraint on when the attack can be attempted.

equipment.rationale: A web browser and a free intercepting proxy (e.g., Burp Suite Community Edition) are sufficient.

threats.notes: Corresponds to OWASP API Security Top 10 2023, API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization. Real-world precedent: Sam Curry et al.'s 2022 mass-disclosure across roughly 16 OEMs (Kia, Honda, Nissan, Hyundai, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Ferrari, Toyota, Ford, Porsche, and others), where VIN-keyed API calls alone were sufficient to remotely unlock, start, locate, and flash the lights of vehicles the researchers did not own.

threats.name: Compromised Aftermarket OBD-II Dongle
threats.description: An insurance, fleet-tracking or diagnostic dongle stays plugged into the OBD-II port and exposes it over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or cellular. An attacker who exploits or impersonates the dongle's radio link sends diagnostic and bus messages through the OBD-II port without touching the vehicle.

elapsedTime.rationale: Weak pairing or unauthenticated firmware updates on popular dongles have been found and exploited within days.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires proficient knowledge of Bluetooth / Wi-Fi pairing and OBD-II messaging.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Dongle models and their protocols are commercially available and documented by researchers.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The dongle must be installed by the owner or fleet operator; the attacker needs radio range (Bluetooth / Wi-Fi) for the duration of the attack.

equipment.rationale: A laptop or phone with a Bluetooth / Wi-Fi adapter.

threats.name: Gather Target Information - from Other
threats.description: The adversary gathers information by directly targeting sources that do not involve the vehicle itself, such as OEM supply chains, surface/dark web, engineering manuals, or breach reports.

elapsedTime.rationale: OSINT and web-scraping queries return results within minutes to hours.

specialistExpertise.rationale: OSINT and web scraping require basic to intermediate IT skills.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The goal is to acquire knowledge; starting knowledge is minimal.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Internet-based research has an unlimited window.

equipment.rationale: Requires only a browser and internet access.

threats.name: Gather Target Information - from Vehicle
threats.description: The adversary gathers information by targeting a vehicle's hardware and/or communication environment to extract firmware, map network topologies, or identify component vulnerabilities.

elapsedTime.rationale: Extracting firmware and mapping network topology from a physical or bench ECU takes days.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires intermediate reverse-engineering and protocol-analysis skill to interpret extracted firmware and traffic.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Diagnostic protocols (UDS) and common extraction techniques are publicly documented; only the target's specific firmware content is discovered through the attack itself.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Requires prolonged physical access to a target vehicle or purchased test-bench ECU.

equipment.rationale: A commodity diagnostic interface and JTAG adapter are sufficient.
